Check the [**assumptions**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} - What sampling distribution are you using? What assumptions are required for it? 2. Set the [**level of significance**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} $\alpha$ 3. Specify the [**null**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} ( $H_0$ ) and [**alternative**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} ( $H_A$ ) [**hypotheses**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} - In symbols and/or in words - Alternative: one- or two-sided? 4. Calculate the [**p-value**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} based on the observed test statistic and its sampling distribution 7. Write a [**conclusion**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} to the hypothesis test - Do we reject or fail to reject $H_0$? - Write a conclusion in the context of the problem ## Steps for hypothesis test for population **slope** $\beta_1$ (using t-test) ::: columns ::: {.column width="48%"} 1. Check the [**assumptions**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} 2. Set the [**level of significance**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} - Often we use $\alpha = 0.05$ 3. Specify the [**null**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} ( $H_0$ ) and [**alternative**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} ( $H_A$ ) [**hypotheses**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} - Often, we are curious if the coefficient is 0 or not: ```{=tex} \begin{align} H_0 &: \beta_1 = 0\\ \text{vs. } H_A&: \beta_1 \neq 0 \end{align} ``` 4. Specify the test statistic and its [**distribution under the null**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} - The test statistic is $t$, and follows a Student's t-distribution. ::: ::: {.column width="4%"} ::: ::: {.column width="48%"} 5. Calculate the [**test statistic**]{style="color:#4FADF3"}. - The calculated **test statistic** for $\widehat\beta_1$ is $$t = \frac{ \widehat\beta_1 - \beta_1}{ \text{SE}_{\widehat\beta_1}} = \frac{ \widehat\beta_1}{ \text{SE}_{\widehat\beta_1}}$$ when we assume $H_0: \beta_1 = 0$ is true. 6. Calculate the [**p-value**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} - We are generally calculating: $2\cdot P(T > t)$ 7. Write a [**conclusion**]{style="color:#4FADF3"} - We (reject/fail to reject) the null hypothesis that the slope is 0 at the $100\alpha\%$ significiance level. There is (sufficient/insufficient) evidence that there is significant association between ($Y$) and ($X$) (p-value = $P(T > t)$). ::: ::: ## Standard error of fitted slope $\widehat\beta_1$ ![](../img_slides/pause.png){.absolute top="1%" right="0%" width="120" height="120"}     ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} $$\text{SE}_{\widehat\beta_1} = \frac{\widehat{\sigma}}{s_X\sqrt{n-1}}$$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} $\text{SE}_{\widehat\beta_1}$ is a measure of **variability** of the estimate $\widehat\beta_1$ ::: :::     ::: {style="font-size: 90%;"} ::: columns ::: {.column width="32%"} - $\widehat{\sigma}$ is the standard deviation of the residuals ::: ::: {.column width="1%"} ::: ::: {.column width="32%"} - $s_X$ is the sample standard deviation of the explanatory variable $X$ ::: ::: {.column width="1%"} ::: ::: {.column width="32%"} - $n$ is the sample size, or the number of observations in the model ::: ::: ::: ## Calculating standard error for $\widehat\beta_1$ (1/2) ![](../img_slides/pause.png){.absolute top="1%" right="0%" width="120" height="120"} - **Option 1:** Calculate using the formula ```{r} glance(model1) # standard deviation of the residuals (Residual standard error in summary() output) (s_resid <- glance(model1)$sigma) # standard deviation of x's (s_x <- sd(gapm$cell_phones_100, na.rm=T)) # number of pairs of complete observations (n <- nobs(model1)) (se_b1 <- s_resid/(s_x * sqrt(n-1))) # compare to SE in regression output ``` ## Calculating standard error for $\widehat\beta_1$ (2/2) ![](../img_slides/pause.png){.absolute top="1%" right="0%" width="120" height="120"} - ::: ::: ## Confidence interval for population **slope** $\beta_1$ Recall the general CI formula: $$\widehat{\beta}_1 \pm t_{\alpha, n-2}^* \cdot SE_{\widehat{\beta}_1}$$ To construct the confidence interval, we need to: - Set our $\alpha$-level - Find $\widehat\beta_1$ - Calculate the $t_{n-2}^*$ - Calculate $SE_{\widehat{\beta}_1}$ ## Calculate CI for population **slope** $\beta_1$ (1/2) ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} $$\widehat{\beta}_1 \pm t^*\cdot SE_{\beta_1}$$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} where $t^*$ is the $t$-distribution critical value with $df = n -2$. ::: ::: - **Option 1:** Calculate using each value Save values needed for CI: ```{r} b1 <- model1_b1$estimate SE_b1 <- model1_b1$std.error ``` ```{r} nobs(model1) # sample size n (tstar <- qt(.975, df = n - 2)) ``` Use formula to calculate each bound ```{r} (CI_LB <- b1 - tstar*SE_b1) (CI_UB <- b1 + tstar*SE_b1) ``` ## Calculate CI for population **slope** $\beta_1$ (2/2) ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} $$\widehat{\beta}_1 \pm t^*\cdot SE_{\beta_1}$$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} where $t^*$ is the $t$-distribution critical value with $df = n -2$. ::: ::: - **Option 2:** Use the regression table ```{r} tidy(model1, conf.int = T) %>% gt() %>% tab_options(table.font.size = 40) %>% fmt_number(decimals = 3) ``` ## Interpreting the coefficient estimate of the population slope with CIs - When we report our results to someone else, we don't usually show them our full hypothesis test - In an informal setting, someone may want to see it - Typically, we report the estimate with the confidence interval - From the confidence interval, your audience can also deduce the results of a hypothesis test - Once we found our CI, we often just write the interpretation of the coefficient estimate: ::: definition ::: def-title General statement for population slope inference ::: ::: def-cont For every increase of 1 unit in the $X$-variable, there is an expected/average (pick one) increase of $\widehat\beta_1$ units in the $Y$-variable (95%: LB, UB). ::: ::: - **In our example:** For every additional cell phone per 100 people, life expectancy increases, on average, `r round(tidy(model1)$estimate[2], 3)` years (95% CI: `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.low[2], 3)`, `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.high[2], 3)`) ## Usually three options for your interpretations - Estimate the variance of the residuals 2. Using a hypothesis test, determine if there is enough evidence that population slope $\beta_1$ is not 0 (applies to $\beta_0$ as well) ::: lob 3. Calculate and report the estimate and confidence interval for the population slope $\beta_1$ (applies to $\beta_0$ as well) ::: 4. Calculate and report the estimate and confidence interval for the expected/mean response given $X$ ## Inference for the population **slope**: hypothesis test and CI ::: columns ::: {.column width="45%"} ::: fact ::: fact-title Population model ::: ::: fact-cont *line + random "noise"* $$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot X + \varepsilon$$ with $\varepsilon \sim N(0,\sigma^2)$\ $\sigma^2$ is the variance of the residuals ::: ::: ::: proposition ::: prop-title Sample best-fit (least-squares) line ::: ::: prop-cont $$\widehat{Y} = \widehat{\beta}_0 + \widehat{\beta}_1 \cdot X $$ Note: Some sources use $b$ instead of $\widehat{\beta}$ ::: ::: ::: ::: {.column width="5%"} ::: ::: {.column width="50%"}   We have two options for inference: 1. Conduct the **hypothesis test** ```{=tex} \begin{align} H_0 &: \beta_1 = 0\\ \text{vs. } H_A&: \beta_1 \neq 0 \end{align} ```
*Note: R reports p-values for 2-sided tests* 2. Construct a **95% confidence interval** for the **population slope** $\beta_1$
::: ::: ## Confidence interval for population **slope** $\beta_1$ Recall the general CI formula: $$\widehat{\beta}_1 \pm t_{\alpha, n-2}^* \cdot SE_{\widehat{\beta}_1}$$ To construct the confidence interval, we need to: - Set our $\alpha$-level - Find $\widehat\beta_1$ - Calculate the $t_{n-2}^*$ - Calculate $SE_{\widehat{\beta}_1}$ ## Calculate CI for population **slope** $\beta_1$ (1/2) ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} $$\widehat{\beta}_1 \pm t^*\cdot SE_{\beta_1}$$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} where $t^*$ is the $t$-distribution critical value with $df = n -2$. ::: ::: - **Option 1:** Calculate using each value Save values needed for CI: ```{r} b1 <- model1_b1$estimate SE_b1 <- model1_b1$std.error ``` ```{r} nobs(model1) # sample size n (tstar <- qt(.975, df = n - 2)) ``` Use formula to calculate each bound ```{r} (CI_LB <- b1 - tstar*SE_b1) (CI_UB <- b1 + tstar*SE_b1) ``` ## Calculate CI for population **slope** $\beta_1$ (2/2) ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} $$\widehat{\beta}_1 \pm t^*\cdot SE_{\beta_1}$$ ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} where $t^*$ is the $t$-distribution critical value with $df = n -2$. ::: ::: - **Option 2:** Use the regression table ```{r} tidy(model1, conf.int = T) %>% gt() %>% tab_options(table.font.size = 40) %>% fmt_number(decimals = 3) ``` ## Interpreting the coefficient estimate of the population slope with CIs - When we report our results to someone else, we don't usually show them our full hypothesis test - In an informal setting, someone may want to see it - Typically, we report the estimate with the confidence interval - From the confidence interval, your audience can also deduce the results of a hypothesis test - Once we found our CI, we often just write the interpretation of the coefficient estimate: ::: definition ::: def-title General statement for population slope inference ::: ::: def-cont For every increase of 1 unit in the $X$-variable, there is an expected/average (pick one) increase of $\widehat\beta_1$ units in the $Y$-variable (95%: LB, UB). ::: ::: - **In our example:** For every additional cell phone per 100 people, life expectancy increases, on average, `r round(tidy(model1)$estimate[2], 3)` years (95% CI: `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.low[2], 3)`, `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.high[2], 3)`) ## Usually three options for your interpretations - **Option 1:** For every additional cell phone per 100 people, life expectancy increases, **on average**, `r round(tidy(model1)$estimate[2], 3)` years (95% CI: `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.low[2], 3)`, `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.high[2], 3)`)   - **Option 2:** For every additional cell phone per 100 people, **average** life expectancy increases `r round(tidy(model1)$estimate[2], 3)` years (95% CI: `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.low[2], 3)`, `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.high[2], 3)`)   - **Option 3:** For every additional cell phone per 100 people, **expected** life expectancy increases `r round(tidy(model1)$estimate[2], 3)` years (95% CI: `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.low[2], 3)`, `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.high[2], 3)`) ## Poll Everywhere Question 4 ## For reference: quick CI for $\beta_0$ - Calculate CI for population **intercept** $\beta_0$: $\widehat{\beta}_0 \pm t^*\cdot SE_{\widehat{\beta}_0}$ where $t^*$ is the $t$-distribution critical value with $df = n -2$ - Use the regression table ```{r} tidy(model1, conf.int = T) %>% gt() %>% tab_options(table.font.size = 40) %>% fmt_number(decimals = 3) ``` ::: definition ::: def-title General statement for population intercept inference ::: ::: def-cont The expected outcome for the $Y$-variable is ($\widehat\beta_0$) when the $X$-variable is 0 (95% CI: LB, UB). ::: ::: - **For example:** The average life expectancy is `r round(tidy(model1)$estimate[1], 2)` years when the number of cell phones per person is 0 (95% CI: `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.low[1], 2)`, `r round(tidy(model1, conf.int = T)$conf.high[1], 2)`). # Learning Objectives 1. Estimate the variance of the residuals 2. Using a hypothesis test, determine if there is enough evidence that population slope $\beta_1$ is not 0 (applies to $\beta_0$ as well) 3. Calculate and report the estimate and confidence interval for the population slope $\beta_1$ (applies to $\beta_0$ as well) ::: lob 4. Calculate and report the estimate and confidence interval for the expected/mean response given $X$ ::: ## Finding a mean response given a value of our independent variable ```{r} #| echo: false tidy(model1) %>% gt() %>% tab_options(table.font.size = 40) %>% fmt_number(decimals = 3) ``` $$\widehat{\textrm{life expectancy}} = `r round(tidy(model1)$estimate[1], 3)` + `r round(tidy(model1)$estimate[2], 3)` \cdot \textrm{cell phones} $$ - What is the expected/predicted life expectancy for any country with 60 cell phones per 100 people? $$\widehat{\textrm{life expectancy}} = `r round(tidy(model1)$estimate[1], 3)` + `r round(tidy(model1)$estimate[2], 3)` \cdot 60 = `r round( tidy(model1)$estimate[1] + tidy(model1)$estimate[2]*60, 3)`$$ ```{r} (y_60 <- tidy(model1)$estimate[1] + tidy(model1)$estimate[2]*60) ``` - How do we interpret the expected value? - We sometimes call this "predicted" value, since we can technically use a number (of cell phones) that is not in our sample - How variable is it? ## Mean response/prediction with regression line ::: columns ::: {.column width="55%"} Recall the population model: *line + random "noise"* $$Y = \beta_0 + \beta_1 \cdot X + \varepsilon$$ with $\varepsilon \sim N(0,\sigma^2)$
- When we take the expected value, at a given value $X^*$, the average expected response at $X^*$ is: $$\widehat{E}[Y|X^*] = \widehat\beta_0 + \widehat\beta_1 X^*$$ ::: ::: {.column width="45%"} ```{r} #| echo: false #| fig.height: 8.0 #| fig.width: 9 gapm %>% ggplot(aes(x = cell_phones_100, y = life_exp)) + geom_point(size=2) + labs(x = "Number of cell phones per 100 people", y = "Life expectancy (years)", title = "Life expectancy vs. cell phones") + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, size =3, color = "#F14124") + geom_vline(xintercept = 60, color = "#A7EA52", size = 3) + theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 27), axis.text = element_text(size = 25), title = element_text(size = 25)) ``` ::: ::: - These are the points on the regression line - The mean responses have variability, and we can calculate a CI for it, for every value of $X^*$ ## CI for population mean response ($\widehat{E}[Y|X^*]$ or $\mu_{Y|X^*})$ $$\widehat{E}[Y|X^*] \pm t_{n-2}^* \cdot SE_{\widehat{E}[Y|X^*]}$$ $$SE_{\widehat{E}[Y|X^*]} = \widehat{\sigma} \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(X^* - \overline{X})^2}{(n-1)s_X^2}}$$ - $\widehat{E}[Y|X^*]$ is the predicted value at the specified point $X^*$ of the explanatory variable - $\widehat{\sigma}^2$ is the sd of the residuals - $n$ is the sample size, or the number of (complete) pairs of points - $\overline{X}$ is the sample mean of the explanatory variable $x$ - $s_X$ is the sample sd of the explanatory variable $X$
- Recall that $t_{n-2}^*$ is calculated using `qt()` and depends on the confidence level ($1-\alpha$) ## Example Option 1: CI for mean response $\mu_{Y|X^*}$ **Find the 95% CI's for mean life expectancy for 60 cell phones per 100 people:** ```{r} #| echo: false Xstar <- 60 Y60 <- tidy(model1)$estimate[1] + tidy(model1)$estimate[2]*60 tstar <- qt(.975, df = n - 2) s_resid <- glance(model1)$sigma n <- nobs(model1) mx <- mean(gapm$cell_phones_100, na.rm=T) s_x <- sd(gapm$cell_phones_100, na.rm=T) SE_Yx <- s_resid *sqrt(1/n + (Xstar - mx)^2/((n-1)*s_x^2)) MOE_Yx <- SE_Yx*tstar LCI = Y60 - MOE_Yx UCI = Y60 + MOE_Yx ``` ```{=tex} \begin{align} \widehat{E}[Y|X^*] &\pm t_{n-2}^* \cdot SE_{\widehat{E}[Y|X^*]}\\ `r round(Y60, 3)` &\pm `r round(tstar, 3)` \cdot \widehat{\sigma} \sqrt{\frac{1}{n} + \frac{(X^* - \bar{x})^2}{(n-1)s_X^2}}\\ `r round(Y60, 3)` &\pm `r round(tstar, 3)` \cdot `r round(s_resid, 3)` \sqrt{\frac{1}{`r n`} + \frac{(`r Xstar` - `r round(mx, 3)`)^2}{(`r n`-1)`r round(s_x, 3)`^2}}\\ `r round(Y60, 3)` &\pm `r round(tstar, 3)` \cdot `r round(s_resid*sqrt((1/n) + ((Xstar - mx)^2)/((n-1)*s_x^2)), 3)`\\ `r round(Y60, 3)` &\pm `r round(tstar * s_resid*sqrt((1/n) + ((Xstar - mx)^2)/((n-1)*s_x^2)), 3)`\\ (`r round(LCI, 3)` &, `r round(UCI, 3)`) \end{align} ``` ## Example Option 2: CI for mean response $\mu_{Y|X^*}$ **Find the 95% CI's for mean life expectancy for 60 and 80 cell phones per 100 people, respectively.** - Use the base R `predict()` function - Requires specification of a `newdata` "value" - The `newdata` value is $X^*$ - This has to be in the format of a data frame though - with column name identical to the predictor variable in the model ```{r} newdata <- data.frame(cell_phones_100 = c(60, 80)) newdata ``` ::: columns ::: {.column width="50%"} ```{r} predict(model1, newdata=newdata, interval="confidence") ``` ```{r} #| echo: false pred_x60 = predict(model1, newdata=newdata, interval="confidence") %>% as.data.frame() ``` ::: ::: {.column width="50%"} ::: fact ::: fact-title Interpretation ::: ::: fact-cont We are 95% confident that the **average** life expectancy for a country with a 60 cell phones per 100 people will be between `r round(pred_x60$lwr[1], 2)` and `r round(pred_x60$upr[1], 2)` years. ::: ::: ::: ::: ## Poll Everywhere Question 5 ## Confidence bands for mean response $\mu_{Y|X^*}$ - Often we plot the CI for many values of X, creating **confidence bands** - The confidence bands are what ggplot creates when we set `se = TRUE` within `geom_smooth` - Think about it: for what values of X are the confidence bands (intervals) narrowest? ```{r} #| fig-align: center #| output-location: column #| fig-height: 8 #| fig-width: 11 gapm %>% ggplot( aes( x=cell_phones_100, y=life_exp ) ) + geom_point() + geom_smooth(method = lm, se=TRUE) + labs( x = "Cell phones per 100 people", y = "Life expectancy (years)", title = "Life expectancy vs. cell phones" ) ``` ## Width of confidence bands for mean response $\mu_{Y|X^*}$ - \bar{x})^2}{(n-1)s_x^2}} \end{align} ``` ```{r} #| echo: false #| fig-align: center gapm %>% ggplot(aes(x = cell_phones_100, y = life_exp)) + geom_point(size = 4) + geom_smooth(method = "lm", se = TRUE, size = 3, colour="#F14124") + labs( x = "Cell phones per 100 people", y = "Life expectancy (years)", title = "Life expectancy vs. cell phones" ) + theme(axis.title = element_text(size = 20), axis.text = element_text(size = 20), title = element_text(size = 17)) + geom_vline(xintercept = mx, color = "purple", size = 3) ``` ## Textbook readings -
